newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's legislature will end with reforms - Prodi.
newsitem.headline: Italy's legislature will end with reforms - Prodi.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi said in an interview to be published on Thursday that his government would step down once Italians had approved a new electoral law.

Parliament has embarked on a reform of Italy's constitution to try to end Italy's history of weak and ineffectual government, but any new legislation is not expected to be in place before 1999 at the earliest.

"I have said I would lead a government for a full term. Well, it's clear that the institutional reform process closes the legislature. That is the way it is, by definition," Prodi told Sette magazine, according to an advance copy.

Prodi's coalition, in office since May 1996, is Italy's 55th government since World War Two. The prime minister has told reporters in the past that he expected his centre-left administration would survive a normal five-year term.

A special parliamentary commission last week finished initial work on a five-point plan of draft changes involving a bigger role for an elected president, an updated constitution, smaller houses of parliament and some judicial reforms.
The proposals have to be ratified twice by both houses of parliament before being fully approved, and they are likely to meet a torrent of amendments.
Once parliament has given the go-ahead to the reform, it still has to be approved by a referendum before becoming law.
Prodi told reporters while on a visit to Spain that the whole business could drag on indefinitely.
"The reforms are never finished," he joked.
The current commission is the third such body set up by parliament in recent years to oversee constitutional reform. The two previous assemblies both failed to produce anything.

At the heart of the latest recommendations are plans to introduce a directly-elected president who will have powers over defence and foreign affairs, replacing the current largely ceremonial position of president.
A prime minister, chosen by the ruling coalition, will oversee domestic policy, while more power will be devolved to Italy's regions.
Sette quoted Prodi as saying he welcomed the reform process. "May it come as soon as possible, even if that means ending the experience of government."
